land.text: the Bajío, where Hidalgo issued the Grito de Dolores, with the cells in Querétaro, Celaya, San Miguel and Guanajuato

predecessors.note: The insurgents took land from the Viceroyalty of New Spain; Cliopatria draws the Spanish Empire there.

land.text: independent Mexico: Iturbide's Army of the Three Guarantees, which Guerrero joined, entered Mexico City on 27 September 1821

successors.note: Cliopatria's insurgent row stops in 1819; the pages carry the insurgency to the independence of 1821, when its remnants merge into the Trigarante movement and the First Mexican Empire.

capitals.name: Guadalajara
capitals.note: Hidalgo set up headquarters at Guadalajara in December 1810 (page).

capitals.name: Zitácuaro
capitals.note: The Supreme National American Junta was installed on 19-21 August 1811 and is named for Zitácuaro; the page does not state its seat. Calleja occupied Zitácuaro on 1 January 1812, and no page opened says where the Junta sat until the Congress of 1813.

capitals.name: Chilpancingo
capitals.note: The Supreme National Congress was 'convened on 14 September 1813' at Chilpancingo.

capitals.name: Apatzingán
capitals.note: The Congress was 'gathered in the city of Apatzingán', where it promulgated the constitution on 22 October 1814, 'due to pursuit by Calleja's troops'. No page gives a seat after the Congress ended in 1815.

correction.text: the Bajío, Valladolid (Morelia) and Guadalajara, the cities the insurgents held in 1810

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1810-1810, a year Cliopatria leaves empty: the Bajío where the Grito de Dolores was raised on 16 September, Guanajuato (the Alhóndiga, 28 September), Valladolid (17 October) and Guadalajara (11 November; Hidalgo's headquarters in December). Radii are my reading of 'held a city', not a boundary from a page.

145,000 km2 (Guerrero 53,000, Michoacán 40,000, Guanajuato 12,000, Querétaro 7,000 and smaller parts by the gazetteer) fits the pages: Morelos 'occupied Chilpancingo on 24 May 1811 and Tixtla on 26 May' (Morelos page), the Junta was installed on 19-21 August 1811 (this page), and Rayón 'fled south on 26 March 1811' after Hidalgo's defeat. The Guanajuato and Querétaro parts are not dated by any page (unverified). No infobox area exists for the insurgents.

264,000 km2 adds Oaxaca (82,000), Puebla and Veracruz to the 1811 shape. The Morelos page dates Tehuacán (10 August 1812), Orizaba (late October 1812, surrendered without bloodshed) and Oaxaca ('He entered Oaxaca in triumph on 25 November 1812'), which explain the growth. Michoacán stays in the shape although Calleja occupied Zitácuaro on 1 January 1812 (Rayón page); the pages do not say how much of Michoacán the insurgents still held. The shape holds to 1813 (Acapulco fell 12 April 1813).

311,000 km2 adds Hidalgo (15,000), more of Puebla and Veracruz (18,000) and a little of México: unverified: page budget. The pages show retreat, not growth, in 1814: a 'series of defeats began at Valladolid in late 1813' (Morelos page), and the Congress had to leave Chilpancingo for Apatzingán 'due to pursuit by Calleja's troops', promulgating the constitution on 22 October 1814. The page also says the constitution was 'valid for insurgent forces in the territories that it controlled' and lists seventeen provinces, without saying which were held. Victoria's band in Puebla (Mexican War of Independence page) may explain the eastern part. Keep the shape as the insurgent claim and treat it as soft.

correction.text: unchanged for 1815; 1816-1819 are described by mexicans_1816

keyframe_review.note: 311,000 km2 stands for 1815 only. After the Congress was dissolved and 'Morelos was captured 5 November 1815' (executed 22 December 1815, Morelos page), the Mexican War of Independence page says 'From 1816 to 1820, the insurgency was stalemated, but not stamped out', fought 'by guerrilla forces in the tierra caliente'; 1816-1821 is mexicans_1816.

correction.text: Guerrero's army at Tixtla and Victoria's band in Puebla: the guerrilla redoubts of the stalemate of 1816-1820

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1816-1821 (Cliopatria stops at 1819): the stalemate left the insurgents 'by guerrilla forces in the tierra caliente (hot country) of southern Mexico'; Victoria arose 'in Puebla' and Guerrero 'in the village of Tixla' (Guerrero state). The page does not say where either held out; in December 1820 Apodaca sent Iturbide 'to defeat Guerrero's army in Oaxaca', so Oaxaca may belong to the redoubt too (not added). The map should show a small hatched rebel area, not the 311,000 km2 of 1815.

region.text: the Bajío: Dolores, San Miguel, Celaya, Guanajuato

ledger.note: 16 September 1810: Hidalgo raises the Grito de Dolores. 'Hidalgo issued his call to arms, the Grito de Dolores' in the Bajío, with the cells in Querétaro, Celaya, San Miguel and Guanajuato. The insurgent movement is the state; Cliopatria's row starts in 1811.

28 September 1810: the rebels take Guanajuato. They 'took on Spanish forces at the Alhóndiga de Granaditas and killed more than 500 Spaniards'; the page does not say in so many words that the city was held.

17 October 1810: Valladolid falls to the rebels. 'Valladolid (October 17), and Guadalajara (November 11) among them' fell to the rebels; the sentence gives no year, but its paragraph opens with 'the Grito de Dolores of Miguel Hidalgo on September 16, 1810'.

11 November 1810: Guadalajara falls to the rebels ('Guadalajara (November 11)', same sentence as Valladolid; year from the paragraph's 1810). The Mexican War of Independence page has Hidalgo setting up headquarters there in December, 'and a month of massacres followed'.

Early 1811: the north is lost. Royalists beat Hidalgo's forces at the Calderón bridge (no date on the page); Rayón 'fled south on 26 March 1811 to continue the fight'; Allende, Jiménez and Aldama 'were executed on 26 June 1811' and Hidalgo on 30 July 1811. The land lost is the 1810 gains, my reading.

24-26 May 1811: Morelos holds the south. 'He occupied Chilpancingo on 24 May 1811 and Tixtla on 26 May.' (He had taken Acapulco in December 1810 except the Fort of San Diego and lifted the siege in January.)

19-21 August 1811: the insurgents form a government. 'From August 19 to 21' Rayón, Liceaga, Joaquín López, Sixto Verduzco and others created the Supreme National American Junta (Junta de Zitácuaro), with Rayón as president; Morelos 'agreed to become a member' and sent Verduzco in his place.
1 January 1812: the royalists take Zitácuaro. 'On January 1, 1812, Zitacuaro was attacked by general Félix María Calleja'; 'When Calleja knew that the city was open, he occupied it.'
10 August 1812: Morelos wins at Tehuacán. 'Tehuacán was a major victory on 10 August 1812' (the page says a victory, not the city's capture).
Late October 1812: Orizaba surrenders. 'Orizaba also surrendered without bloodshed in late October 1812.'

25 November 1812: Morelos enters Oaxaca. 'He entered Oaxaca in triumph on 25 November 1812.' The page names the city; the whole state is my reading, matching Cliopatria's 1812 shape (82,000 km2 of Oaxaca).

region.text: the port of Acapulco, without the Fort of San Diego

ledger.note: 12 April 1813: Acapulco falls to Morelos. 'Acapulco fell on 12 April 1813, forcing the Spanish army to take refuge in the Fort of San Diego.' (The Calleja page has 20 April 1813.)
14 September 1813: the Congress meets at Chilpancingo. 'Proclaimed as the Supreme National Congress, it was convened on 14 September 1813.' Rayón's post in the Junta ended on 13 September 1813.

6 November 1813: the Congress declares independence. 'On 6 November 1813, the Congress declared independence.' (The Sentimientos de la Nación, undated on the page, abolished slavery and racial categories.)

22 October 1814: the Constitution of Apatzingán. The Congress, 'gathered in the city of Apatzingán' 'due to pursuit by Calleja's troops', promulgated a constitution that 'declared that Mexico would be a Republic'; the Supreme Government was three persons (Cos, Liceaga, Morelos).

minus.text: Guerrero's army at Tixtla and Victoria's band in Puebla: the guerrilla redoubts of the stalemate of 1816-1820

region.text: the insurgent land outside the guerrilla redoubts of Guerrero and Puebla

ledger.note: 1816: the insurgents are reduced to guerrillas. 'After the dissolution of the Congress of Chilpancingo, Morelos was captured 5 November 1815' and shot on 22 December 1815 (Morelos page); 'From 1816 to 1820, the insurgency was stalemated, but not stamped out.' The page does not say what land was lost; the royalists get all but the guerrilla redoubts (my reading).

region.text: Guerrero's army at Tixtla and Victoria's band in Puebla: the guerrilla redoubts of the stalemate of 1816-1820

ledger.note: 1821: Guerrero joins Iturbide. Iturbide, sent against Guerrero in December 1820, contacted him in January 1821 and 'persuaded Guerrero to join his forces in support of this conservative independence movement'; the Plan of Iguala was proclaimed on 24 February 1821. The page gives no date for Guerrero's acceptance.

region.text: Guerrero's army at Tixtla and Victoria's band in Puebla: the guerrilla redoubts of the stalemate of 1816-1820

ledger.note: 27 September 1821: independence. The Treaty of Córdoba 'recognized Mexican independence' (24 August) and 'On 27 September 1821, the Army of the Three Guarantees entered Mexico City'; the insurgents' war ends with the independence they had declared in 1813.

wars.name: Mexican War of Independence

zones.text: the insurgent-held land at its largest as Cliopatria draws it

wars.outcome: Independence in 1821 by the Plan of Iguala (24 February) and the Treaty of Córdoba (24 August); the insurgent government itself was crushed in 1815 and the war stalemated 1816-1820.
wars.note: The New Spain dossier records the matching contest from 1810 to 1821.

wars.name: Siege of Cuautla
wars.outcome: Morelos 'broke through the siege' on 2 May 1812 after 58 days (Morelos page); the Mexican War of Independence page says 72 days under Calleja.
wars.note: No border moved; listed because the siege shaped the 1812 campaigns.

wars.name: Mina expedition
wars.outcome: Mina 'and 300 men landed at Rio Santander' in Tamaulipas in April 1817 and fought seven months until captured in November 1817.
wars.note: A foreign expedition in support of the independence cause; no territory held.

certainty.note: The insurgents held cities and districts, not surveyed frontiers; the pages name no boundary. The 1816-1821 redoubts are the softest.

sources.title: José María Morelos

sources.note: The Congress of Chilpancingo (14 September 1813), Apatzingán (22 October 1814), Article 42's provinces, the Supreme Government.

sources.note: The Supreme National American Junta (19-21 August 1811), Calleja at Zitácuaro (1 January 1812), Rayón's term as deputy to 15 December 1815.

notes:
WHAT THIS IS. Cliopatria's 'Mexicans' (1811-1819) is the insurgent side of the Mexican War of Independence; its Wikipedia title is the ethnic-group article, which was not opened (the war, Morelos, Apatzingán, Rayón and Calleja were). The dossier is type 'rebel' (rule 5) and follows the movement from the Grito de Dolores (16 September 1810) to independence (27 September 1821), since Cliopatria's 1811-1819 span leaves out the Bajío phase of 1810 and the guerrilla years 1820-1821. The New Spain dossier (am-06-x) records the matching contest 1810-1821 against 'mexicans'.

NOT SETTLED. (1) The Bajío phase of 1810 is four cities and a region; radii are my reading. (2) 1814: Cliopatria's 311,000 km2 (more Puebla, Veracruz and Hidalgo than 1812) is unverified; the pages show retreat. (3) 1816-1821: the pages say 'stalemated' and 'guerrilla forces in the tierra caliente' but not where; the correction is Guerrero plus the Puebla part of Cliopatria's shape (Guerrero 'in the village of Tixla', Victoria 'in Puebla'); Oaxaca is mentioned for December 1820 only. (4) Where the Junta sat in 1812-1813 and what the insurgents held in Michoacán after Zitácuaro (Jan 1812) is not on the pages; Rayón's fort at Jaujilla, the Junta's moves (Sultepec) and the Cuautla siege dates were asked of the pages and are not there. (5) The 'Mexicans' successor in 1821 is Iturbide's Army of the Three Guarantees; Cliopatria's 'First Mexican Empire' starts in 1822, so 1821 has no shape: the 'first-mexican-empire' dossier (another part) should say who held the land in 1821 or start that state in 1821.

DISAGREEMENTS. Siege of Cuautla: 72 days (Mexican War of Independence page) vs 58 days to 2 May 1812 (Morelos page). Acapulco: 12 April 1813 (Morelos) vs 20 April 1813 (Calleja). Morelos's capture: 5 November 1815 (Mexican War of Independence, Morelos pages); the Calleja page puts 'capture and subsequent execution' on 22 December 1815. The Congress: dissolved before 5 November 1815 (Mexican War of Independence page) vs Rayón a deputy to 15 December 1815 (Rayón page). Abolition etc. are not territorial.

GAZETTEER. Not found: Zitácuaro, Tixtla, Cuautla, Dolores Hidalgo (places); 'Tierra Caliente' (region). Zitácuaro and Cuautla are given as lon/lat radii; Tixtla is covered by the Chilpancingo radius. Valladolid is resolved as Morelia.
